articles.summary: Alcon in Action: Strengthening Communities Around the World sandra.hoffer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 15:52 Story Headline Alcon in Action: Strengthening Communities Around the World Story Teaser Summary Since its launch in 2012, Alcon in Action (AiA) has empowered associates around the world to give back to the communities where they live and work. From helping build homes in Texas to engaging with seniors in Germany, AiA creates opportunities for associates to make a meaningful impact through service. While every project looks different, each reflects Alcon’s commitment to strengthening communities and helping people Live Brilliantly. Story Date Thu, 11/05/2026 - 12:00 Featured 1 Category Vision for the World Hero image For Alcon associates around the world, making a difference begins close to home. Through Alcon in Action (AiA) , Alcon’s annual global volunteer initiative, associates use their time and skills to support communities where they live and work. Activities are tailored to local needs and carried out in partnership with community organizations. So far in 2026: More than 5,100 Alcon associates contributed 16,468 volunteer hours Volunteers supported 132 organizations across 72 Alcon sites Activities included: 24 education activities 26 housing projects 19 environmental health activities Complementing these AiA efforts, Alcon's Matching Gifts and Volunteer Incentive Program gives associates flexibility in how they give back, matches donations to eligible nonprofits. Meeting Communities Where They Are In Fort Worth, Texas, Alcon associates’ impact included working with Trinity Habitat for Humanity to help build three homes in the Garden Springs community. In 2026, nearly 250 associates contributed more than 1,700 volunteer hours to the project as part of the site’s annual AiA activities. The three German Wavelight sites in Erlangen, Pressath, and Teltow offer a variety of volunteer opportunities throughout the year from supporting schools to improving playgrounds, allowing associates to participate in ways that fit their interests. Some of the most memorable moments have come from simple human connection. For example, associates accompanied residents from a nursing home on a visit to a local soccer stadium where they were able to meet the team mascot. Associates have also stepped in to support renovation projects at schools and kindergartens where limited community budgets meant extra help was especially valuable. "For me, the best part is seeing people come together, learn from each other, and create something positive. Sometimes it's a renovated room, sometimes a child's excitement about learning something new, and sometimes it's simply a meaningful conversation that stays with you long after the day is over." Steffi Igler, Health, Safety and Environment associate and Alcon in Action site lead for Germany That sentiment is shared at Alcon's Sinking Spring, Pennsylvania, site where associates regularly engage with nonprofit organizations in their community. Site leader Sara Galosi works closely with Alcon's social impact teams to coordinate volunteer opportunities for approximately 100 associates each year and partners with eight to 10 different nonprofit organizations. In 2026, Sinking Spring associates supported nine volunteer activities spanning hunger, health, housing and education. Their work has included cooking and serving meals at homeless shelters, sorting donations, preparing food boxes, supporting a local food bank, assisting with senior programs and helping prepare an Easterseals camp for the summer. For Galosi, volunteering has also offered a closer look at challenges that may exist only a few miles from the workplace. She got to see firsthand the impact AiA can make while volunteering at a local mobile market close to the Alcon facility. "This experience opened my eyes to the widespread issue of food insecurity and the many neighbors who are affected. It was a powerful reminder of the importance of our work and the difference we can make in people's lives." Sara Galosi, Manufacturing and Technical Operations associate and Alcon in Action site lead for Sinking Spring, Pennsylvania Creating Connection in Singapore At Alcon's Singapore sites, AiA’s participation has grown from around 80 volunteers in 2022 to around 140 volunteers in 2026. Associates from manufacturing, commercial and regional teams have been involved in activities addressing areas including hunger, environmental sustainability, health and community well-being. In 2025, associates spent time with seniors, accompanying them on grocery shopping trips, a particularly meaningful and engaging experience for the AiA volunteers. Building on that positive experience, leaders built the 2026 program around a similar opportunity to support seniors living on Pulau Ubin, a small island located off the northeastern coast of mainland Singapore, providing practical supplies, environmental clean-up efforts and eye health education. Associates also partnered with the National Parks Board on coastal cleanup efforts, removing approximately 250 kilograms of waste. "AiA has shown me that the most valuable things we can give are often intangible, such as our time, attention and genuine care. It is heartwarming to see the community enjoying the experience and our associates leaving happy, fulfilled and proud of what they achieved together. Our growing volunteer turnout is a ‘good headache’ because it shows that more people want to step forward, connect with the community and make a meaningful difference." Ivy Cheam, Legal and Compliance associate and Alcon in Action Site Lead for Singapore Looking Ahead Alcon sites around the world are focused on expanding participation and strengthening community partnerships, building on years of impact through AiA. From supporting food banks and schools to spending time with seniors and improving local outdoor spaces, the activities may look different from one Alcon site to another, but they all have a shared purpose to help people Live Brilliantly. articles.summary: Not Everything That Looks Real Is Real: How AI Is Changing Fraud angela.wan+a Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:54 AI fraud is the use of artificial intelligence to make scams more realistic and harder to recognize. Scammers can use AI to imitate voices, create convincing images and videos, write polished messages or build fake websites — all designed to gain your trust and potentially steal money or personal information. The holiday season often brings the moments we look forward to all year: finding the perfect gift, gathering with family and friends and checking items off our shopping lists. Unfortunately, it also brings an increase in fraud and scam activity. Many of the tactics themselves aren't new. What's changing are the tools fraudsters can use to make them more believable. A message can look professional. A website can appear legitimate. Even a familiar voice may not be what it seems. According to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) , consumers and businesses across the United States reported more than $20 billion in internet crime losses in 2025, highlighting the growing scale and sophistication of fraud nationwide. The technology may be changing, but the objective remains the same: gain your trust, create urgency and persuade you to act before taking time to think. That makes independent verification increasingly important, even when a request looks or sounds real. How AI Is Making Fraud More Convincing Traditional scams often contained clues that something wasn't right: awkward language, spelling mistakes, unusual formatting or a message that simply didn't sound like the person or company supposedly sending it. Artificial intelligence can make some of those clues less obvious. Generative AI can help fraudsters write polished emails and text messages, while voice-cloning technology can make a caller sound like someone you know. Deepfake technology can create realistic-looking video or audio, and AI can also help criminals develop professional-looking websites, advertisements and online profiles. These tools can support social engineering, in which scammers manipulate people into sharing information, sending money or taking another action. The result is an important shift in how we think about fraud prevention: something looking professional or sounding familiar isn't necessarily proof that it's legitimate. Common Types of AI Fraud and How They Work AI-powered scams can take many forms, but the goal is often similar: create enough trust or urgency to convince the victim to act before verifying the request. Here are some scenarios to watch for. The Voice That Sounded Familiar: AI Voice Cloning Let's say you're a grandparent. The phone rings, and your grandchild is on the other end. They sound upset and say they were in an accident while traveling. They need help and ask if you can send money immediately. They plead with you not to tell anyone else. The voice sounds familiar, the story feels believable and your first instinct is to help. While scams like these are not new, artificial intelligence is making them more convincing. Fraudsters can use AI voice-cloning technology to imitate a person's voice and create calls designed to appear genuine and earn your trust. The urgency and secrecy are important warning signs. Before sending money or sharing sensitive information, contact the person directly using a trusted phone number or reach out to another family member to verify the story. The Deal That's Too Good to Pass Up: Fake Shopping Websites You find the perfect gift online at an incredible price. The website looks professional, the photos are convincing and the customer reviews appear genuine. Excited to secure the deal, you place the order. Artificial intelligence can help fraudsters build fake websites, realistic product descriptions, convincing advertisements and believable customer reviews. Scammers may also use QR codes in advertisements, emails, social media posts or promotional materials to direct shoppers to fraudulent websites designed to collect payment or personal information. Before purchasing from a link you found on social media, take a few moments to research the seller and verify the website URL. Exercise caution when scanning QR codes that direct you to payment or login pages. If a deal seems too good to be true, it probably is. The Package You're Waiting For: AI-Powered Phishing A package delivery notification arrives by text message. The message says a package is delayed and updated payment information is needed before delivery can be completed. It includes a convenient link to resolve the issue. Because many of us are expecting deliveries during the holidays, these messages can appear legitimate. Phishing is a type of scam in which criminals impersonate a trusted person or organization to persuade someone to provide information, click a malicious link or take another action. Generative AI can make phishing emails and text messages more polished and personalized, potentially making an AI scam more difficult to recognize based on language alone. When tracking a package, navigate directly to the retailer's or shipping carrier's website rather than clicking links in unexpected messages. Deepfake Impersonation and Fake Investment Scams A familiar face can create the same sense of trust as a familiar voice, and deepfake technology can be used to create realistic-looking fake video or audio of another person. In deepfake scams, fraudsters may impersonate public figures, financial professionals, company executives or other trusted individuals. For example, fabricated videos, endorsements or online profiles could be used to make an investment opportunity appear legitimate. Scammers may combine these materials with fake investment platforms or websites to reinforce the story and encourage a person to transfer money or provide financial information. Before acting on an investment offer or unexpected financial request, independently verify both the person making the request and the organization involved. A convincing video, voice or online profile should not substitute for verification. For Businesses: The Payment Request That Appears Routine An employee receives an email that appears to come from a trusted supplier. The request seems straightforward: update payment instructions to send a payment to a new account. Everything looks legitimate. Artificial intelligence is helping fraudsters create polished business communications that are free of obvious spelling or grammar mistakes. This can make fraudulent payment requests harder to distinguish from legitimate ones. Before processing payment changes, businesses should independently verify requests using established contact information and follow existing approval procedures. Warning Signs of AI Fraud Because AI-enabled scams can appear polished and realistic, identifying fraud may require looking beyond spelling mistakes or poor-quality images. Potential warning signs include: Urgent requests to send money or provide sensitive information Pressure to keep a request secret or act immediately Unexpected changes to payment instructions Requests for passwords, one-time passcodes, login credentials or verification codes Requests to use unusual payment methods or send money to unfamiliar accounts Links, email addresses or website URLs that don't match the organization being impersonated Requests to bypass normal verification or approval procedures Unexpected communications asking for financial information or account access No single warning sign necessarily means a communication is fraudulent. At the same time, the absence of obvious mistakes doesn't establish that a request is legitimate. When something unexpected involves money, account information or personal data, taking time to verify it through a separate, trusted channel can help you determine what you're really dealing with. How to Protect Yourself From AI Fraud As AI technology evolves, the fundamentals of fraud prevention remain useful: pause, verify and protect your information. Here are five practical steps you can take. 1. Verify Requests Through Trusted Channels If you receive an unexpected call, email or text asking you to send money, change payment information or provide account details, independently verify the request. Contact the person or organization using a phone number or website you already know or have independently located. Don't rely on the phone number, link or contact details provided in the suspicious message itself. This extra step can be particularly important when a request involves an urgent money transfer or changes to banking information. 2. Create a Family Verification Plan Consider establishing a family code phrase that can be used to verify someone's identity during an emergency request. If a caller claims a relative is in trouble, contact that person directly or check with another family member before taking action. With voice cloning making it possible to imitate familiar voices, hearing someone who sounds like a loved one may no longer be enough to confirm their identity. 3. Protect Your Personal and Banking Information Never share passwords, one-time passcodes or verification codes with someone who contacts you unexpectedly. Be cautious about entering account or financial information through unfamiliar links, and use available account security features. Regularly reviewing your account activity may also help you identify transactions you don't recognize. For more practical steps, review Cathay Bank's cybersecurity tips to help you stay safe and information about bank cybersecurity trends and protection . 4. Be Cautious With Links, QR Codes and Online Offers Instead of following an unexpected link, navigate directly to the organization's official website. Research unfamiliar retailers and investment opportunities before providing payment information. Check website addresses carefully, particularly before entering login credentials, banking details or other sensitive data. QR codes deserve the same caution as other links. You may not know where a QR code will take you until you scan it. 5. Limit Information That Could Be Used for Impersonation Think about how much personal information, including photos, videos and audio recordings, is publicly available through social media. Scammers may use publicly available data to make impersonation attempts more convincing. Reviewing privacy settings and being thoughtful about what you share publicly can reduce the amount of information readily available to someone attempting to build a convincing story about you or someone you know. What To Do If You Receive a Suspicious Message or Request If something doesn't feel right, stop before taking the requested action. Don't click additional links, send money or provide more information. Instead, independently contact the person, business or financial institution supposedly making the request using trusted contact information. If the communication involves your Cathay Bank account, banking information or a transfer, contact Cathay Bank using a trusted number, such as the number on the back of your card. If you've already shared information or believe fraudulent activity may have occurred, contact your financial institution for guidance on appropriate next steps. You can also learn more about how to protect yourself when banking online. Scams and other internet crimes can be reported to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center. Frequently Asked Questions About AI Fraud What Is AI Fraud? AI fraud involves using artificial intelligence to facilitate or make fraudulent activity more convincing. It may include AI-generated messages, voice cloning, deepfakes, fake websites and other techniques intended to deceive people into sharing information, sending money or taking another action. Can Scammers Use AI To Copy Someone's Voice? Yes. Voice-cloning technology can create audio that imitates a person's voice. Scammers may use this technology in impersonation scams, including fake emergency calls involving family members. Independently contacting the person through a trusted number can help you verify whether the request is genuine. How Can You Tell if a Message Is an AI Scam? There may not always be an obvious visual or grammatical clue. Watch for behaviors commonly associated with scams, including unusual urgency, secrecy, unexpected requests for money or information and pressure to bypass normal verification. When you're uncertain, independently contact the person or organization through a trusted channel rather than replying directly to the suspicious communication. What Should You Do If You Think You've Been Targeted by AI Fraud? Stop interacting with the suspicious communication and independently verify the request. If the situation involves banking or financial information, contact your financial institution through a trusted number for guidance on appropriate next steps. Pause. Verify. Protect. Whether it is a familiar voice, an online shopping bargain, a package notification, a deepfake or a business payment request, scammers often succeed by creating urgency and encouraging quick decisions. Artificial intelligence is making scams more convincing. From realistic voices to sophisticated websites and polished emails, not everything that looks real is real. If you receive an unexpected call, text message, email or notification, take a moment to verify before taking action. Contact organizations through trusted phone numbers or websites, and never share one-time passcodes or verification codes with someone who contacts you unexpectedly. The holidays should be about spending time with family and friends, not recovering from fraud. If something feels off, trust your instincts. articles.summary: Testing & Evaluation in the Agentic Age: Watch the Recording Building an AI agent is only half the challenge. Knowing whether you can trust it in production is where the real work begins. The recording of our AI Expert Circle session, Testing & Evaluation in the Agentic Age, is available. The session explores a fundamental shift in how we need to think about quality: from testing whether software produces the expected output to continuously evaluating agent behavior and building evidence that supports greater autonomy. ▶ Watch the recording What we covered The session looks at several practical building blocks for testing and governing GenAI and agentic solutions: Golden reference datasets: establishing evaluation baselines that make it possible to compare the behavior of prompts and agents consistently. Repeatable evaluation: comparing different prompts, contexts, and agent variants rather than relying on one-off testing. Multi-signal evaluation: combining human feedback and SME annotations with technical metrics, process outcomes, and business signals. Silent evaluation: collecting production evidence without introducing operational risk before increasing an agent's autonomy. Human-in-the-Loop patterns: using human involvement as part of a deliberate progression from assisted toward more autonomous operation. Governance and monitoring: continuing evaluation beyond go-live rather than treating testing as a one-time release gate. ▶ Watch the recording Three key takeaways 1. Agentic AI changes what “testing” means. Traditional pass/fail testing works well when an application is deterministic. GenAI and agentic systems can produce multiple plausible outcomes from the same input, so evaluation needs to consider performance and behavior over time rather than validating only one expected answer. 2. Trust should be based on multiple forms of evidence. No single metric tells you whether an agent is ready. The session explores combining SME judgment, human feedback, technical measures, process outcomes, and business signals to create a stronger basis for rollout and governance decisions. 3. Autonomy should be earned through evidence. Silent evaluation, SME annotations, Human-in-the-Loop patterns, and ongoing monitoring provide ways to gather evidence before expanding autonomy. From testing prompts to governing behavior Perhaps the most important shift is this: the objective isn't simply to prove that an agent worked in a test. It is to establish an ongoing evidence loop that helps us understand when, where, and under which conditions we can trust it. If you are building agentic solutions, leading delivery teams, or defining AI governance approaches, watch the recording for practical techniques and reusable patterns for designing, validating, monitoring, and governing AI systems. ▶ Watch the recording Continue the conversation If you’re working through similar questions around testing, evaluation, Human-in-the-Loop, or governing increasingly autonomous agents, we’d love to hear what you’re encountering in practice. And if you’d like to discuss how these approaches might apply to your own use cases, please reach out to me or Glen Aronson. We’re always happy to exchange ideas, compare approaches, and learn from what others are seeing in the field.

articles.summary: If you trade US stock tokens on Mudrex, you may occasionally come across a corporate action called a stock split or reverse stock split. These are normal events that happen to real, listed companies, and because your Mudrex position tracks the price of the underlying stock, your position gets adjusted too. This can look surprising if you don’t know it’s coming, so here’s a quick breakdown of what these events are, what happens on Mudrex when they occur, and whether you need to do anything about it. What is a stock split? A stock split increases the number of shares a company has outstanding while reducing the price per share by the same ratio. The total value of what a shareholder holds doesn’t change; it’s just divided into more, cheaper units. Companies typically do this to bring their share price down to a more accessible range for investors. Example: In a 10-for-1 stock split, every 1 share becomes 10 shares, and the price per share drops to roughly one-tenth of what it was. If you held 1 share worth $100 before the split, you’d hold 10 shares worth $10 each after it, same total value. What is a reverse stock split? A reverse stock split does the opposite: it reduces the number of shares outstanding while increasing the price per share by the same ratio. Companies usually do this to raise their share price, often to meet a listing requirement or improve how the stock is perceived in the market. Example: In a 1-for-10 reverse split, every 10 shares get consolidated into 1 share, and the price per share increases to roughly 10 times what it was. If you held 10 shares worth $10 each before, you’d hold 1 share worth $100 after- again, the same total value. Why does this affect my Mudrex position? Your US stock token on Mudrex is a contract that tracks the price of the underlying stock; it isn’t the actual share itself. So when the real company’s share count and price change because of a split, Mudrex adjusts your position to keep it accurately tracking the stock, using the same ratio as the actual corporate action. Timeline: What to Expect About 7 days before the adjustment The stock split or reverse split is announced publicly by the company and reflected on Mudrex. This gives you advance notice before anything changes on your position. During the adjustment (roughly 30 minutes) At the scheduled time, trading on the affected asset is briefly paused while the position adjustment is carried out. You won’t be able to open, close, or modify positions on that asset during this window. This window is typically around 30 minutes but may occasionally take a little longer if needed. Once the adjustment is complete Trading resumes automatically. Your position quantity and average entry price will now reflect the new, post-split numbers. What happens to your position Your position quantity and average entry price will change. This is expected and matches the split ratio; your position’s overall value stays consistent with the adjustment. It isn’t a gain or loss caused by the split itself. Any open orders, including Stop Loss (SL) and Take Profit (TP) orders, will be automatically cancelled at the start of the adjustment. This is a routine part of how the adjustment is processed, not an error. A small amount may be settled as a gain or loss. If your position size doesn’t divide evenly under the new ratio, a small leftover portion is settled at the prevailing market price so the rest of your position can be adjusted cleanly. This shows up in your position history as a distinct “Split Adjustment” entry with no fee charged. Your position will not be liquidated as a result of the adjustment itself. Positions on the affected asset are frozen and protected from liquidation for the duration of the adjustment window. Normal liquidation risk based on your account margin resumes once trading reopens. Your trade history from before the adjustment is not affected. Any orders that were cancelled during the adjustment will still be visible in your Order History, marked as cancelled, so you can review and re-place them if needed. Steps you may need to take Re-place your Stop Loss / Take Profit orders after trading resumes, since these are cancelled during the adjustment and are not automatically restored. Review your adjusted position (quantity and average entry price) once trading resumes, to confirm it lines up with what you expect. Check your Order History if you had open orders on the asset, to see which ones were cancelled and decide whether to re-place them. Check your position history if you notice a small unfamiliar PnL entry around the time of the adjustment; it’s likely the split settlement described above. No action is needed during the adjustment window itself; trading will resume on its own once the process is complete. A few things to keep in mind Mudrex US stock tokens are price-tracking contracts. Holding one does not give you ownership of the underlying stock or any shareholder rights such as dividends or voting rights. Stock splits and reverse splits are designed to be value-neutral; they change how your holding is denominated (more units at a lower price, or fewer units at a higher price), not what it’s worth. The one exception is the small settlement described above, which can result in a minor gain or loss. As always, keep sufficient margin in your account, since normal market risk and liquidation rules continue to apply once trading resumes.
articles.title: Stock Splits and Reverse Stock Splits: What They Mean for Your US Stock Positions on Mudrex
